newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN agency aiding 3.3 mln Palestinians "bankrupt".
newsitem.headline: UN agency aiding 3.3 mln Palestinians "bankrupt".

text.p: The main United Nations agency aiding 3.3 million Palestinians is "technically bankrupt" at a time when social and economic stability are vital to Middle East peace prospects, its director said on Monday.
Peter Hansen, head of the U.N. Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA), called urgently for $25 million to meet the agency's $312 million budget this year.
"I am facing this year for UNRWA a situation where the agency is technically bankrupt," he told a news conference in Geneva after a fund-raising tour in the Gulf and Southeast Asia.
"We are not going to close tomorrow, but our liabilities exceed our assets. We don't have any working capital," he added.

Major donors including the largest, the United States whose share is $70 million, have paid in. But UNRWA has depleted its reserves to finance deficits four years in a row and is seeking new donors to keep pace with a refugee population which expands by five percent a year, according to the Dane.
UNRWA provides education, health care and social services to 3.3 million Palestinian refugees in Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, the West Bank and Gaza Strip. About one-third live in 59 camps.

Hansen said the income of the 1.3 million Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza Strip had fallen by 40 percent since the peace process began four years ago, mainly because of Israeli closures which prevent Palestinians from working in Israel.

"That means that since the peace process started, the Palestinians have been losing 10 per cent in their living standard every year since then," he said. "People are poorer than they were before. They are in need of more services."
The building of new Jewish settlements in East Jerusalem had also made the work of UNRWA more difficult, according to Hansen.
Hansen's fund-raising tour in Asia included stops in Malaysia, Indonesia and Brunei and he was hopeful of donations.

Last month he went to five Gulf countries (Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates). "We think the Gulf countries can do a little more," he said, noting they contribute about one percent of the agency's regular budget.

"It is absolutely necessary to increase our donor base so that we will be able to continue delivering this very important programme in this very important part of the world where stability is a precondition for any hope of progress towards peace," Hansen said.
